INDEPENDENT
Independent of the usual axioms of set theory (ZFC).
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal with $\aleph_0<\mathfrak{m}<\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}$. Let $\{f_\alpha\}$ be a family of entire functions such that, for every $z_0\in \mathbb{C}$, there are at most $\mathfrak{m}$ distinct values of $f_\alpha(z_0)$. Must $\{f_\alpha\}$ have cardinality at most $\mathfrak{m}$?
#1119: [Ha74]
analysis | 
set theory
This is Problem 2.46 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.
Erdős [Er64g] proved (answering a question of Wetzel) that if there are only countably many distinct values for each $f_\alpha(z_0)$ then, if $\mathfrak{c}>\aleph_1$, the family $\{f_\alpha\}$ is itself countable, and also showed this is false if $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$. 
In [Ha74] it is written that it is 'easy to see' the answer is yes if $\mathfrak{m}^+<\mathfrak{c}$, and also that it is possible that the question is undecidable.
Indeed, it has been shown that this is undecidable if $\mathfrak{m}^+=\mathfrak{c}$: Kumar and Shelah [KuSh17] have shown that there is a model in which $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$ such that the answer is yes (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_1$), while Schilhan and Weinert [ScWe24] have shown the answer can be no, in a different model with $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$.

 For the maximal case $\mathfrak{m}^+ = \mathfrak{c}$, Theorem 2.1 of Kumar and Shelah's On a question about families of entire functions (2017) establishes that within the Cohen real model obtained by adding $\aleph_2$ Cohen reals to the constructible universe $L$ (so $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_2$ there), every continuum-sized family of entire functions takes $\mathfrak{c}$ distinct values at some point $z$. Consequently, by the contrapositive, any family that takes at most $\mathfrak{m}$ distinct values at every point cannot be continuum-sized (as the theorem would require it to have $\mathfrak{c}$ values at some point); it must have cardinality $\leq \mathfrak{m}$. Therefore, the answer to Problem 1119 is "YES" for the maximal case $\mathfrak{m} = \aleph_1$ in this model. The authors note in Question 4.1 that a model where the answer is "NO" for the maximal case (e.g., $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_2$) was an open question.
However, Schilhan and Weinert in Wetzel families and the continuum (2024) answered this open question asked by Kumar and Shelah, proving the answer can be "NO" in a different model where $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$​.
This resolves the problem completely: the answer is known to be "YES" for $\mathfrak{m}^+ < \mathfrak{c}$ and undecidable for $\mathfrak{m}^+ = \mathfrak{c}$.
Also in the problem statement, $m$ should be replaced with $\mathfrak{m}$.
